COVID-19: Elderly - Dying of Loneliness

By: Kate Barry | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Is Covid killing the elderly in Old Age Homes or are they dying from loneliness in lockdown?

Unique Selling Point:
Interview with Nico Steytler, son of the late Elsa Joubert, who wasn't allowed to see his mother for 3 months. On the day she was diagnosed with Covid-19 he wheeled her from Berghof Retirement Home across the road to the Life Hospital. She disappeared through the Casualty doors and he never saw her again.
Two weeks before her death Die Burger published a letter from Elsa on the front page, pleading for the elderly to be allowed to see their families. The pain of separation from loved ones was making their last weeks and days a living hell.


Summary:
Covid-19 poses a greater risk to people over the age of 60, and lockdown measures are meant to keep them safe. Ironically the virus has swept through South Africa's Old Age Homes and retirement villages anyway, leaving death and destruction in its wake. Many residents, management and staff have fallen ill, many have died. While most South Africans are straining under the economic pressures of lockdown restrictions, we are still allowed some freedom of movement. But for the elderly the boredom and loneliness of being locked down without visits from loved ones now poses a severe threat to their mental health.
We ask what is the true situation in our old age homes?
Has the response from the provincial and National governments been sufficient?
How did the virus enter the facilities?
Do residents have access to social workers to deal with the loneliness of isolation?
Is it fair to continue to keep them separated from their families?

Further information:
Jaffa House in Pretoria has had 10 deaths due to Covid-19.
The Greek Old Age Home in Johannesburg has had 9 deaths due to Covid-19
Deansgate in Craighall Park has had 4 deaths.
Sandringham Gardens and Our Parents Home have also had a number of Covid-19 infections and deaths.
The situation in these Homes are mirrored in hundreds of facilities throughout the country. We have asked all the above for an interview, and are waiting to see which Home will allow us access to management, staff and residents.

Brigitte Helmrich Daughter
Nico Steytler Son of Elsa Joubert
Daniela Chrysostomou Chairwoman: Greek Ladies Benevolent Society

Dr. Leon Geffen Director: Samson Institute for Ageing Research

Script:


DYING OF LONELINESS

V/O: It’s Monday afternoon in Johannesburg and Brigitte Helmrich is visiting her 90-year-old mother Inge at the German Old Aged Home.

Sfx: Chatter

Shouting above the noise of the traffic might not be ideal, but it’s the only contact they’re allowed under the lockdown restrictions.

Brigitte: Nobody goes inside and nobody goes outside. They have been kept isolated since March. But I know she’s safe. It would be lovely to hug her it would be lovely hold her but it’s not doable at the moment.

Link: It’s unnatural to talk to a parent over a wall or through a fence – especially for 5 months. It’s no wonder the elderly feel like they’ve been imprisoned. But it’s a scene that has played out all over the country and all over the world. The tragedy is the virus gets in anyway.

V/O: On the 14th of June Covid claimed the life of South African literary icon Elsa Joubert. The author of Poppie Nongena lived at Berghof, a retirement home in Cape Town. When lockdown came, she too was cut off from family and friends.

Nico: We obviously used the telephone, but then the complication was that because of her age her hearing wasn’t very good.

V/O: Her son Nico Steytler feels angry that he couldn’t be there for his mother.

Nico: Why is it so harsh? The rules don’t make sense. This is where you felt most needed – the last days, the last years – this is where your value as a child really comes in - to look after them - and then suddenly no.

V/O: At the age of 97 Elsa became a voice for the elderly, writing a letter to Die Burger pleading for time with her children and grandchildren. But it was only when she got sick that Nico was allowed into the Home for the first time in 3 months.

Nico: You put on the full protective gear. We had a wonderful talk, still our last whiskey, but the next day I then wheeled her literally across the road. And then suddenly the real isolation hits you.

V/O: Nico was not allowed into the hospital and had to say goodbye to his mother at the door.

Nico: There was no fear in her, and she faced it and seven days later she died.

V/O: Dr Leon Geffen is an expert in the field of ageing and is on the WHO task committee that drafted the guidelines on infection control of Covid in care facilities

Leon: It is terrible not to be able to have direct access to loved ones, but one’s got to weigh that up against the safety of residents; trying to protect their wellbeing and their health and trying to mitigate the effects that Covid would have if it spreads though a facility.

Derek: Do we know how the mental health of these residents has been affected?

Leon: I think what the lockdown’s impact has been is in those people who generally don’t do well under healthy or normal circumstances, are not going to do well now. Those people who are fairly resilient and do well, find their ways to manage the process.

Willie: It all depends on the individual, like I’m very positive. If I was not well, I wanted to get better.

V/O: 96-year-old Willie Pokroy lives at JAFFA House in Pretoria. He was one of 39 residents who contracted Covid in June.

Willie: I was tested positive and I was in isolation for about two weeks and thereafter I was clear. I get up every morning and I say thank you I’m here.

V/O: The Home went into full lockdown with residents confined to their rooms.

Mark: Nobody came out of their rooms for 14 days, we isolated, staff in full PPE. We had doctors come in daily to monitor, and they advised us that as it went on, people were turning symptomatic take them to hospital.

V/O: Despite their best efforts 11 residents died from Covid; the loss has been traumatic, says Director Mark Isaacs.

Mark: As much as I’ve tried here to protect people, it got in. Ja, you know it really got to me.

V/O: Strict social distancing measures are still in place, and for the last 2 months the only contact with family has been through an iPad or a dedicated Zoom room.

Maish: It’s not a nice thing, but I think the whole world is suffering at the moment.

Derek: What’s been the worst time for you?

Maish: Being with people that you see every day and all of a sudden, they’re gone. I found it very, very hard.

V/O: But now loved ones are allowed to visit at the fence. Today Maish and Bella Jaffe are seeing their son Neil for the first time in two months – at a distance of 6 metres.

Derek: It must be difficult Neil?

Neil: It’s very difficult, upsetting for everybody involved because you like to touch your parents; you want to give them a hug, you want to give them some emotional support and we just couldn’t do that, and we still can’t do that.

V/O: Bridget Masango is the DA’s Shadow Minister for Social Development. She believes the government could have done more to assist the elderly during this crisis.

Bridget: We have in this country over 4000 unemployed social workers that have been trained by government and obtained 4-year degrees to be social workers. You would have thought those would be deployed in these homes for the elderly to provide psychosocial support. Now we are told that these elderly are falling. The incidence of falling is increasing which means that they need some physical exercise and things like that, and the government hasn’t done anything like that.

Derek: It just doesn’t make sense that there are people qualified to help them and they’re not being used?

Bridget: You would have read that the government was employing 1800 of those social workers. More than I think 10 of those young people wrote to me and said we were told to go to SASSA and the Post Office and we were used as queue marshals at pay-points.

V/O: In a written response the Department acknowledged ideally all Homes should have a dedicated Social Worker, but that budget constraints don’t allow it.

Link: We may have moved to Level 2 of the lockdown, but the old age homes are not taking any chances. The stringent rules regarding protective equipment and visitors still remain. Now hopefully they will help to protect the lives of the residents, but will they love long enough to survive the lockdown?

Leon: I think it’s time to allow a slightly more open approach to care facilities. It’s five months that people have effectively been in lockdown, and I think we need to allow these things to happen now.

Liana: Your active ageing is decreasing - meaning your loneliness and depression - those things increased because we isolated them.

V/O: Liana Grobler is President of the South African Association of Homes for the Aged, representing over 420 homes nationwide.

Liana: All the homes has been affected. As far as we know there is not one home that has not experienced a Covid case.




V/O: Full PPE was required before we could enter The Greek Old Age Home in Johannesburg. They managed to keep the virus at bay during Level 5 of the lockdown.

Daniela: Everybody slept in for a solid 5 weeks. I think the staff had suffered a lot. They’ve got families, they’ve got kids. They’re young people they’ve children at home. They had to leave everything to sacrifice themselves and be here with the elderly to look after them..

V/O: But when the country moved to Level 4, they also suffered a Covid outbreak according to Daniela Chrysostomou.

Daniela: We did lose 4 residents here at the home, and 5 they passed away in the hospital. The staff and the residents, we are a big family and if one of them dies of course it’s hurting.

Derek: Were any of them able to see their families before they passed on?

Daniela: No, we locked up again.

Link: Many of the elderly who tested positive for coronavirus did not survive and lie buried in our cemeteries. But it’s difficult to give accurate figures.

V/O: If someone died at home without being tested for Covid, it wasn’t recorded as a Covid death. This could explain the huge spike in so-called excess deaths last month. According to the Medical Research Council reported Covid deaths spiked in mid-July, but so did deaths from Natural Causes.

Leon: I think we’re undercounting very significantly. We know from the MRC data that’s been well published in terms of the expected number of deaths in the country and the total number of deaths, that the total number of deaths are well above that which is expected. And the only rational explanation for that is probably Covid-related deaths.

V/O: To improve Covid records, the Department of Health now requires all persons who die at home to be tested for the coronavirus, before a Death Certificate is issued.

Derek: How do you keep up the spirits here?

Daniela: I give them Greek music. I get them to dance.

Sfx: Music

Daniela: We celebrate life every day because we don’t know what tomorrow will bring.

Sfx: Music.

Daniela: We don’t know which one of us will go by tomorrow, so we celebrate today.
